summaries.example: Imagine two teams building weather models. Both models predict tomorrow’s rain correctly, but one team says its hidden picture of the clouds is exactly real, while the other says only that the model works for what we can observe. The second team’s attitude is closer to constructive empiricism.
summaries.summary: Constructive empiricism is a view about what science is trying to do. It says science aims to create theories that fit the observable world. A theory is empirically adequate when what it says about observable things and events is correct. The view does not say that scientific theories are meaningless stories or that scientists should reject them. Instead, theories may be understood literally and used seriously while a person believes only that they fit the observable evidence. The person can remain unsure about unobservable parts, such as hidden entities or structures described by the theory. This differs from scientific realism, which says science aims at truth about both observable and unobservable reality. Constructive empiricism also says that accepting a theory includes a practical commitment: scientists use it to guide research and face new observations. The theory may help with experiments, descriptions, and explanations without proving that every invisible part of its picture is real. The view is influential, but philosophers disagree about whether it correctly describes science, how to draw the observable line, and whether its account of theory acceptance is too cautious or not cautious enough.
key_ideas: Constructive empiricism says that science aims for accurate descriptions of observable parts of the world.
It does not require scientists to believe that every unobservable thing named by a theory really exists.
A theory can be understood literally: its claims can be true or false, and its claims about existence still count.
Scientists may use and explain with a theory even when they remain unsure about its hidden parts.
Choosing a theory can involve practical features such as usefulness, simplicity, and explanatory power.
What counts as observable is not always perfectly clear, especially when instruments such as microscopes are involved.
summaries.why_it_matters: This view helps us separate two questions: “Does a theory work for what we can observe?” and “Is the theory’s whole hidden picture exactly true?” That distinction can encourage careful thinking about evidence and uncertainty. It also explains how scientists might use a theory successfully while still disagreeing about what unobservable parts of the theory really mean. The debate matters because science often discusses things that cannot be seen directly, and we need to think clearly about what evidence supports.

important_terms.definition: The idea that science mainly aims to produce theories that correctly describe what we can observe, not necessarily everything hidden behind what we observe.
Things, events, or patterns that can be observed without using special measuring tools.
A theory’s matching the observable things and events in the world, including ones we have not observed yet.
The view that science tries to give a literally true account of both observable and unobservable parts of the world.
Using a theory as a useful guide and believing it works for observations, without needing to believe every hidden part is real.

questions_to_think_about: If a model makes correct predictions, must its hidden story be true?
Is seeing an image through a microscope the same as seeing the object itself?
Why might scientists choose a simpler or more useful theory?
Can a person use a theory without believing every part of it?

summaries.example: Suppose a particle theory accurately organizes every relevant measurement and helps researchers design new experiments. A scientific realist may say this success is evidence that the theory’s unobservable particles and structures are real. A constructive empiricist can accept the theory as empirically adequate and use it in research while withholding belief about whether its unobservable story is true. The theory can guide work without settling its entire ontology.
summaries.summary:
Constructive empiricism, associated with Bas van Fraassen, is a form of scientific anti-realism. Its central claim is that science aims to provide theories that are empirically adequate: theories whose observable consequences fit the actual observable phenomena. Acceptance of a theory therefore requires belief in its empirical adequacy, together with a practical commitment to use the theory in research, but it need not require belief that the theory is true in its claims about unobservables. This contrasts with scientific realism, which treats science as seeking literal truth about the entire world. Constructive empiricism is not simply instrumentalism or a denial that theories have meaningful content. A theory may be read literally, with genuine truth-or-falsity claims and genuine existence claims. The disagreement concerns the degree of belief warranted by scientific activity, especially regarding unobservable entities and structures.

The view relies on an observable/unobservable distinction, though the entry emphasizes that “observable” is vague and should not be expected to have a perfectly sharp boundary. Unaided observation is central to the original account; viewing an image through a microscope is not straightforwardly observing the microscopic object itself. The entry also discusses empirical adequacy in semantic terms: a theory specifies models, and observable data can fit into the empirical substructure of at least one model. key_ideas: Constructive empiricism is primarily a doctrine about the aim of science, not a rule saying what every individual is rationally permitted to believe.
It contrasts with scientific realism by limiting science’s aim at truth to the observable, while treating unobservable claims with agnosticism if desired.
The view accepts a literal understanding of theories: their claims are truth-apt, and existence claims are not removed by reinterpretation.
Empirical adequacy goes beyond already observed results because it concerns all actual observable phenomena, including possible future observations.
In the semantic account, observable reports can be embedded in the empirical part of at least one theoretical model without requiring belief that the model’s unobservable components exist.
Acceptance combines belief in empirical adequacy with a pragmatic research commitment and can come in degrees.
summaries.why_it_matters: Constructive empiricism gives a precise way to discuss scientific success without assuming that every successful theory is completely true. It highlights the difference between using a theory, believing that it fits observable phenomena, and believing that its unobservable ontology matches reality. That distinction is important in debates about particles, fields, models, and theoretical entities. The position also raises difficult questions about observation, instruments, explanation, and whether science should be characterized by a general aim. Even readers who reject constructive empiricism can use its distinctions to clarify what scientific evidence does and does not establish.

important_terms.definition: Bas van Fraassen’s anti-realist philosophy of science: science aims at empirically adequate theories, and accepting one need not involve belief in its full truth.
A theory is empirically adequate when observable phenomena, including actual phenomena not yet observed, fit within the structures described by at least one of its models.
The claim that science aims at a literally true account of the world, including its unobservable entities and structures.
The distinction between what can be observed by unaided members of an epistemic community and what cannot be observed in that way.
The attitude of believing a theory is empirically adequate while not believing it true or false in its full unobservable claims.
A semantic account on which a theory is represented by a family of models and by empirical substructures that can represent observable phenomena.
A person’s practical commitment to use a theory in research, confront new phenomena through it, and continue a research program.
A philosophical concern about adding commitments to entities such as objective laws, natural kinds, or objective possibilities beyond what empirical science requires.

questions_to_think_about: Does successful prediction support truth about unobservable entities, or only empirical adequacy?
Can the observable/unobservable distinction be useful even if its boundary is vague?
Does using microscope-based information amount to observing microscopic objects?
If a theory is accepted as empirically adequate, what commitments are made about mathematical models?
Should the aim of science be defined by a general goal, or by the many practices scientists actually perform?

summaries.example: Your class has two explanations for why a plant grew quickly. Both correctly predict what students can see: the plant’s height, leaves, and need for water. One explanation adds an invisible story about tiny processes inside the plant. A realist might say the invisible story is probably true because it explains the visible results. A constructive empiricist would say the explanation can be accepted for fitting the observations, while staying unsure whether every hidden part is real.
summaries.summary:
Constructive empiricism is a philosophy of science that asks what science is aiming for. It says science aims at theories that are empirically adequate: theories that correctly describe the observable world. This includes observable events that have not yet been noticed, not just the results already collected. When someone accepts a theory, the person believes that it is empirically adequate and commits to using it in research. The person does not have to believe that the theory’s statements about unobservable things are true.

This differs from scientific realism. A realist says science aims to provide a literally true account of the whole world, including things that cannot be observed. A constructive empiricist can still understand a theory literally. That means the theory makes genuine claims that could be true or false, including claims that something exists. The disagreement is not simply about whether theories are useful stories. It is about how far belief should extend.

The view also separates the aims of science from the personal goals of scientists. A scientist might want recognition or fame, but the philosophical question concerns what makes scientific work successful as science. Experiments can help build or improve theories by finding regularities in observable phenomena. Theory choice may also depend on practical features such as simplicity, scope, elegance, and explanatory usefulness. Constructive empiricists can value these features without treating them as proof that a theory’s hidden claims are true.

key_ideas: Constructive empiricism and scientific realism disagree about what science aims to achieve.
Constructive empiricism focuses on observable success rather than truth about hidden entities.
A theory can be meaningful and literal even if scientists do not believe all its unobservable claims.
Empirical adequacy includes observable phenomena that have not yet been discovered or measured.
Acceptance involves both a belief about adequacy and a commitment to use the theory in future research.
Observation is important but complicated: the boundary between observable and unobservable may be vague, especially with instruments.
summaries.why_it_matters: Constructive empiricism helps students see that “works well” and “is completely true” are different claims. Science often uses models that describe hidden structures, so this distinction affects how we think about evidence, prediction, and scientific progress. The position also explains why scientists can speak confidently within a theory while still disagreeing about its unobservable parts. Its debates show that even familiar words such as “observe,” “explain,” and “accept” can have important philosophical meanings.

important_terms.definition: A view that science aims for theories that fit the observable world, without requiring belief that their claims about unobservable things are true.
A theory’s being correct about observable things and events, including observable events that have not yet been observed.
The view that successful science aims to tell the truth about both observable and unobservable parts of reality.
Something that can be observed without special instruments, according to the relevant community of observers.
Using a theory in research and believing it fits observations, while not necessarily believing its complete story about reality.
A scientific theory’s claims being treated as real statements that can be true or false, rather than being changed into a different kind of statement.
A practical feature of a theory, such as usefulness or simplicity, that can help scientists choose how to work with it.

questions_to_think_about: Is a theory’s ability to explain observations evidence that it is true, or only that it is useful?
Why would a theory need to fit observations that no one has made yet?
Does a microscope show us a tiny object, or an image that needs interpretation?
Can two people accept the same theory while having different beliefs about its hidden parts?
Should simplicity count as evidence for truth, or mainly as a useful reason for choosing a theory?
